title: Undo without guessing
outcome: Choose restore, reset, revert, or reflog from what must be preserved.
cue: Preserve first. Inspect second. Move last.
version: Modern Git; check git --version for command availability

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt: You reset a branch and realize a useful commit disappeared from the log. Recover access without destroying current work.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt: A bad commit is already on a shared branch. Why might revert be easier for teammates than reset plus force-push?

trace.title: Inspect state
trace.detail:
# The idea

Start with the question: what must stay? Working edits, staged changes, published history, and untracked files are different things.

Inspect status and diffs, then preserve important work before experimenting.

restore copies selected content into the index or working tree depending on flags. reset can move a branch and, depending on mode, also change the index and working tree. revert creates a new commit that reverses a past change.

That usually fits a published-history repair better than moving everybody’s history.

The reflog records recent local reference movements. It can help find an old branch tip after reset or rebase.

It is local and expires. It is not a backup of every unsaved file or every other developer’s machine.

trace.title: Follow the middle steps
trace.detail:
A soft reset moves the branch while keeping index/working content. A mixed reset also resets the index.

A hard reset can discard tracked working changes. None should be run by habit.

Recovery starts by naming the old reachable commit with a rescue branch. Inspect it separately.

A deleted untracked file that was never stored in Git is outside reflog’s promise. Seek editor/filesystem backups instead.

trace.title: Check the result
trace.detail:
git clean removes untracked content; reflog may not help. Do not use clean or reset --hard as generic “fix Git” commands.

Reverting a merge also needs a deliberate mainline choice and affects future merge behavior.
